scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Aerial dance emerged in the United States during the 1970s, born from modern dance's exploration of three-dimensional space.
Trisha Brown's equipment pieces from 1968 to 1971 were foundational, using side walls to recontextualize pedestrian movement.
In the 1970s, Terry Sendgraff's motivity trapeze introduced single-point suspension, allowing for rotational movement.
on_screen: Map: United States · Global
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performers present aerial dance at arts festivals, in contemporary circus, and as site-specific installations.
The work explores themes of weightlessness, freedom, and the human relationship with architecture.
Practitioners view it as a place where everything is possible, breaking floor-bound constraints to communicate ideas through an altered state of gravity.
It remains a living tradition today.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers utilize suspended apparatuses to perform wraps, inversions, and drops.
In vertical dance, performers in harnesses use walls as floors, executing leaps and runs perpendicular to the ground.
In silk (tela) work, dancers climb using 'French' or 'spiral' ascents and secure themselves with 'keys' (locks) around the waist or feet.
Watch for Kamikaze, Star drop.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (gLt_4CBdqlA)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Three-dimensional; utilizes vertical, horizontal, and diagonal paths.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music complements the choreography and the rhythm of the apparatus.
While no specific genre is required, contemporary scores, electronic music, and theatrical soundscapes are common.
Listen for synthesizers, percussion, strings, and electronic soundscapes.
The pulse is variable.
The soundscape typically features sweeping electronic or orchestral textures to emphasize the vertical space, punctuated by rhythmic beats that cue drops or transitions.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Settings range from traditional theaters and circus tents to office buildings, bridges, and canyons.
Costumes are form-fitting to avoid entanglement, often using acetato deportivo or jersey fabrics for the apparatus.
Safety equipment is essential, including crash mats, carabiners with screw locks, and swivels for 360-degree rotation.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include Trisha Brown, Terry Sendgraff, Joanna Haigood, Amelia Rudolph, Wanda Moretti, and Isabelle Chassé.
The Boulder style in Colorado is known for its annual festival and workshops.
The discipline combines modern dance, traditional circus arts like Spanish web and static trapeze, and rock climbing.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Aerial dance is a subgenre of modern dance, applying its aesthetics to vertical space.
It includes aerial silk, a discipline using fabric.
It also includes bungee dance, which uses elastic cords for high-rebound movement.

scenes.title: Welcome
narration: Chapter 1 covers first steps. Today, we build core and grip strength.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Engage your core and elongate your limbs, using hollow body positioning for inversions.
High grip strength is required, with arms used for pulling during ascents and stabilizing during poses.
Use your center of gravity for hip keys and controlling rotation.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1 is the French climb or subida francesa.
Step 2 is the foot lock or llave de pie.

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Perform Step A and Step B without stopping, starting slowly.
Move to half tempo, then full tempo.
The instructor mirrors you, so your right is your right.
Drill: practice basic leg wrap mechanics while seated.
